sections.content: Seven days before Yom Kippur they separate (mafrishin) the Kohen Gadol from his house to the Chamber of Parhedrin, and they prepare another kohen in his place lest a disqualification (pesul) befall him (lines 1-4). Rabbi Yehuda: they also prepare another wife for him lest his wife die, as it says 'and he shall atone for himself and for his house' (Lev 16), 'his house' is his wife (lines 4-7). They (the Sages) said to him: if so, there is no end to the matter (line 7). No reply by Rabbi Yehuda appears on this daf.

'Tenan hatam': seven days before the burning of the parah they would separate the kohen who burns it from his house to the chamber facing the Bira, to the northeast, called the Chamber of the Stone House (lines 8-11). Why so called? Because all its acts were done with dung vessels, stone vessels and earth vessels (lines 12-14).

Question: what is the reason (for those vessels)? Answer: since a tevul yom is fit for the parah (line 14), as taught: they would make the kohen who burns the parah tamei and immerse him, to refute the Sadducees who said it was done only by those whose sun had set (me'orvei shemesh) (lines 15-17); the Rabbis instituted dung, stone and earth vessels that do not receive impurity, so that people would not treat it lightly (lines 18-20). The stated cause is the tevul yom leniency; the Mishnah about deliberate impurity is cited as its proof.

Why northeast specifically? Since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and of it is written 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' (Num 19:4), the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a distinguishing sign (heikher) (lines 20-24). Rashi: the parah itself is not slaughtered in the north (it was on the Mount of Olives); the location is a sign, not a fulfillment of a directional requirement.

What is Bira? Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan: a place on the Temple Mount named Bira (lines 24-26). Reish Lakish: the whole Mikdash is called Bira, as it says 'the Bira which I prepared' (I Chr 29:19) (lines 26-27). No resolution.

Menah hanei milei (source for the separation of the Kohen Gadol and of the parah kohen)? Rabbi Manyomi bar Chilkiya citing Rabbi Machsiya bar Idi citing Rabbi Yochanan: 'As was done this day, the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you' (Lev 8:34): 'to do' = acts of the parah, 'to atone' = acts of Yom Kippur (lines 27-31). Challenge: granted the whole verse cannot be set on the parah, since 'to atone' is written and the parah is not a matter of atonement; but say the whole verse is about Yom Kippur (lines 32-34). Answer (amrei): he derives tzivah-tzivah: here 'the Lord commanded to do', there 'this is the statute of the Torah which the Lord commanded' (Num 19:2); as there it is the parah, so here the parah; and as here there is separation, so there separation (lines 34-38). The challenge concedes the Yom Kippur half.

defects.currentClaim: Says the Sages required impurity-proof vessels 'to prevent that provocation from breeding contempt', i.e. that the cause was the deliberate impurity act; omits the Parah Mishnah's seven-day separation and the Stone House naming; presents the derivation as complete without noting the open 've'eima' challenge at line 39.
defects.sourceSupports: Line 14: the stated reason is 'keivan d'tevul yom kasher b'parah' (the tevul yom leniency); lines 15-17 are cited as proof of that leniency; lines 18-20 the vessels prevent the parah being treated lightly. Lines 8-14 cite the parah kohen's separation and the chamber name. Line 39 begins an unresolved challenge.
defects.proposedReplacement: Tractate Yoma opens with the Mishnah's rule that seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is separated from his home to the Chamber of Parhedrin, and another kohen is prepared in case he becomes disqualified; Rabbi Yehuda wants another wife prepared too, lest his wife die, since 'his house' in the verse means his wife, but the Sages answer that if so there is no end to the matter. The Gemara cites the parallel Mishnah in Parah: the kohen who burns the parah adumah is likewise separated seven days beforehand, to the Chamber of the Stone House facing the Bira to the northeast, so called because all its service used dung, stone, and earth vessels. The reason for those vessels is that a tevul yom is fit for the parah (the kohen was even deliberately made tamei and immersed, to refute the Sadducees who required sunset), so the Sages required vessels that cannot become impure, so that people would not treat the parah lightly. The chamber is in the northeast as a distinguishing sign: the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting. Rabbi Yochanan explains 'Bira' as a specific place on the Temple Mount, and Reish Lakish as the whole Temple. Finally, Rabbi Yochanan derives both separations from the inauguration verse 'as the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you': 'to do' is the parah and 'to atone' is Yom Kippur. When the Gemara asks why the whole verse should not refer to Yom Kippur, it answers with a verbal analogy on 'tzivah' linking the verse to the parah statute. The daf ends as the Gemara begins a further challenge ('ve'eima'), which continues on the next daf.

defects.currentClaim: 'Why seven days specifically? And what makes the Sages' response to Rabbi Yehuda more than just 'don't be absurd'?'
defects.sourceSupports: Nothing in lines 1-7 addresses why the number is seven (the inauguration source appears only at lines 27-38, and the seven-day count there comes from Rashi/the verse context). The second question presupposes the Sages' reply is more than a bare objection, contradicting misconceptions[0].correction.
defects.proposedReplacement: If the Mishnah prepares a backup Kohen Gadol, why do the Sages refuse to prepare a backup wife?

defects.currentClaim: Misconception is Rabbi Yehuda's actual tannaitic view; correction calls the Sages' retort 'dismissive rather than a reasoned concession', which is incoherent and contradicts learning.coreMove (a formal rejection).
defects.sourceSupports: Line 7: 'amru lo im ken ein ladavar sof' is a reasoned objection (no end). The Sages do not dispute the derashah 'beito zo ishto' on this daf.

proposedReplacement.misconception: The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda because they deny that 'his house' in the verse means his wife.
proposedReplacement.correction: The Sages do not dispute that derashah in the Mishnah. Their only stated objection is that if one prepares for the wife's death, there is no end to the matter.

defects.proposedReplacement: Seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is separated from his house to the Chamber of Parhedrin, and another kohen is prepared in his place in case a disqualification befalls him.

defects.currentClaim: 'Why stone vessels? Countering the Sadducees on tvul yom'

defects.currentClaim: The vessels prevent 'the provocation from breeding contempt'.
defects.sourceSupports: Line 14: the reason for the vessels is 'keivan d'tevul yom kasher b'parah' (because a tevul yom is fit). Lines 15-17 cite the Mishnah (they made the kohen tamei and immersed him to refute the Sadducees) as proof of that leniency. Lines 18-20: therefore the Rabbis instituted vessels that do not receive impurity 'kei heichi d'lo lizalzelu bah'. Rashi: because a tevul yom is fit, people might think the parah needs little purity, so the Sages added stringencies. The source does not say the vessels repair a problem created by the deliberate impurity act, and does not say people would perform it in impurity.
defects.proposedReplacement: Because a tvul yom is fit to burn the parah, as shown by the practice of deliberately making the kohen tamei and immersing him to refute the Sadducees, the Sages required vessels that cannot become tamei, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.

Because of that leniency, the Sages instituted vessels that cannot receive impurity, so that people would not come to treat the parah lightly.

Since the parah is lenient in this respect, the Sages instituted vessels that cannot receive impurity at all, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.

defects.sourceSupports: The dispute in line 17 concerns the parah specifically ('bim'orvei hashemesh haytah na'aseit'); a tvul yom being unfit for ordinary Temple service is not a Sadducean distinctive.
defects.proposedReplacement: Sadducean position: the parah adumah could be performed only by a kohen whose sun had set after immersion, not by a tvul yom.

defects.currentClaim: 'The parah is a chatat, so its service requires the north side... Northeast is the intersection of both requirements.'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 20-24: 'since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and it is written of it toward the front of the Tent of Meeting, the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a heikher'. The location is a rabbinic sign. Rashi on these lines: this does not mean the parah itself must be in the north; it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives. Nothing says the parah's service requires the north or that the chamber fulfills two requirements.
defects.proposedReplacement: Because the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and of the parah it is written 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' (Numbers 19:4), which points east, the Sages instituted a chamber to the northeast.

defects.sourceSupports: The chatat reason and the verse are on lines 21-22.

defects.currentClaim: 'Two independent Torah requirements point to two different directions; the Sages found a single physical location that satisfies both.'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 20-24: 'since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and it is written of it toward the front of the Tent of Meeting, the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a heikher'. The location is a rabbinic sign. Rashi on these lines: this does not mean the parah itself must be in the north; it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives. Nothing says the parah's service requires the north or that the chamber fulfills two requirements.
defects.proposedReplacement: The parah's chatat status points north and its verse 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' points east, yet neither requires its chamber to be in any place; the Sages chose the northeast to give it a distinguishing sign.

defects.currentClaim: 'Multi-requirement convergence: when two halakhic orientations must be respected, select the intersection point...'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 20-24: 'since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and it is written of it toward the front of the Tent of Meeting, the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a heikher'. The location is a rabbinic sign. Rashi on these lines: this does not mean the parah itself must be in the north; it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives. Nothing says the parah's service requires the north or that the chamber fulfills two requirements.
defects.proposedReplacement: The Sages placed the chamber at the northeast so that its location carries a recognizable sign (heikher) of two scriptural features of the parah: it is a chatat (north) and its verse faces the Tent of Meeting (east).

defects.currentClaim: 'Two independent directional requirements satisfied simultaneously by their geometric intersection.'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 20-24: 'since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and it is written of it toward the front of the Tent of Meeting, the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a heikher'. The location is a rabbinic sign. Rashi on these lines: this does not mean the parah itself must be in the north; it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives. Nothing says the parah's service requires the north or that the chamber fulfills two requirements.
defects.proposedReplacement: Two scriptural features of the parah, its chatat status (north) and facing the Tent of Meeting (east), are signaled together by one rabbinically chosen location, not literally fulfilled by it.

defects.currentClaim: 'It is the precise intersection of two independent halakhic directional requirements...'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 20-24: 'since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and it is written of it toward the front of the Tent of Meeting, the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a heikher'. The location is a rabbinic sign. Rashi on these lines: this does not mean the parah itself must be in the north; it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives. Nothing says the parah's service requires the north or that the chamber fulfills two requirements.
defects.proposedReplacement: The Gemara explains the northeast as a rabbinic choice: the parah is a chatat, a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting; the location serves as a distinguishing sign (heikher), not as the fulfillment of a directional requirement.

defects.currentClaim: '...because the parah adumah is a chatat (north side required) and must face the Tent of Meeting entrance (east).'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 20-24: 'since it is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and it is written of it toward the front of the Tent of Meeting, the Rabbis instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a heikher'. The location is a rabbinic sign. Rashi on these lines: this does not mean the parah itself must be in the north; it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives. Nothing says the parah's service requires the north or that the chamber fulfills two requirements.
defects.proposedReplacement: The Sages instituted that the parah kohen's chamber be to the northeast as a distinguishing sign, since the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting.

defects.currentClaim: '...the two associations the Gemara names at lines 20-23 - nothing on this daf ties it to Yom Kippur's own service.' (reviewer meta text in learner prose)
defects.sourceSupports: Content supported, meta commentary is not learner content.
defects.proposedReplacement: Northeast chamber: north for the parah's chatat status, east for facing the Tent of Meeting; a distinguishing sign (heikher) instituted by the Sages.

defects.sourceSupports: 'Chatat hi v'chatat te'unah tzafon' is on line 21.

defects.currentClaim: Correction asserts 'It is a methodological dispute about how to read Mishnaic geographic terms'.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 24-27 give two definitions of one word; no methodological claim is made or implied in the source.

proposedReplacement.misconception: Both Amoraim agree that 'bira' refers to the whole Temple and differ only about the proof verse.
proposedReplacement.correction: Rabbi Yochanan, quoted by Rabba bar bar Chana, says Bira was a specific place on the Temple Mount; Reish Lakish says the whole Mikdash is called Bira, citing 'the Bira which I prepared'.

defects.currentClaim: '...it is actually a methodological dispute about how to read Mishnaic geographic terms.'
defects.sourceSupports: Unsupported characterization; the source records a definitional dispute about this one word.
defects.proposedReplacement: Students may assume both Amoraim are defining the same kind of thing; Rabbi Yochanan names one specific place on the Temple Mount, while Reish Lakish applies the word to the entire Mikdash.

defects.sourceSupports: Reish Lakish's statement begins on line 26; line 25 is Rabbi Yochanan's.
Reish Lakish's proof verse is on line 27.

defects.currentClaim: Two declarative sentences asserting the answer, then a question: a descriptive paragraph rather than a question.
defects.sourceSupports: Contract: display.hint is a question. Content basis: lines 32-34 concede the parah-only reading fails and ask about a Yom-Kippur-only reading; lines 34-38 answer with tzivah-tzivah.
defects.proposedReplacement: Once 'to atone' rules out reading the whole verse as the parah alone, what does the Gemara use to rule out reading the whole verse as Yom Kippur alone?

defects.currentClaim: States flatly that Lev 8:34 'is the source for both seven-day rules' with no indication that the daf ends opening a further challenge.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 27-31: the derivation is Rabbi Yochanan's (via Rabbi Manyomi bar Chilkiya and Rabbi Machsiya bar Idi); lines 34-38 defend it. The flat 'is the source' presents it as closed, but the discussion continues on the next amud; per the boundary decision the sugya may say only that, without the next amud's content.
defects.proposedReplacement: Rabbi Yochanan derives both seven-day separations from Leviticus 8:34: 'to do' for the parah, 'to atone' for Yom Kippur; a gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' ties the inauguration verse to the parah statute, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

defects.currentClaim: '...ties the milu'im verse's to do to the heifer statute, importing its sequestration requirement. The daf ends with a further objection to this derivation left unanswered.' ('its' reads as the heifer statute's requirement, reversing the direction; and the last sentence rests on line 39, outside the sugya range)
defects.sourceSupports: Line 38: 'as here (inauguration) there is separation, so there (parah) separation': separation flows from the inauguration to the parah. The further objection is on line 39, outside lines 27-38; under the boundary decision s06 may only say the discussion continues on the next amud.
defects.proposedReplacement: The Gemara asks where the seven-day separation comes from. Rabbi Yochanan answers from Leviticus 8:34 (the inauguration passage): 'as He commanded to do, to atone.' 'To do' is read as the parah adumah; 'to atone' is read as Yom Kippur. The whole verse cannot refer to the parah alone, since a parah does not atone. When the Gemara asks why the whole verse should not refer to Yom Kippur, it answers with a gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' (Lev 8:34 and Num 19:2): as there it is the parah, so here it is the parah, and as the inauguration had separation, so the parah requires separation. The discussion continues on the next amud.

defects.currentClaim: Says 'The Gemara finally asks' and 'The answer comes through' without attribution, and ends as if the derivation were closed.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 27-29: the answer is Rabbi Yochanan's via a chain of tradents; the discussion continues on the next amud, which s06 may say without stating its content.
defects.proposedReplacement: The Gemara asks: where does the Torah mandate the seven-day separation at all? Rabbi Yochanan answers from Leviticus 8:34 (the Tabernacle inauguration verse): 'as He commanded to do, to atone.' 'To do' refers to the parah adumah and 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. Granted, the whole verse cannot refer to the parah alone, since 'to atone' is written and a parah is not a matter of atonement; but why can't it all refer to Yom Kippur? The Gemara answers with a gezerah shavah on 'commanded/commanded' (Lev 8:34 and Num 19:2): just as the parah verse there refers to the parah, so too 'commanded' here, in the inauguration verse, refers to the parah; and just as here, at the inauguration, there is separation before the service, so too there, regarding the parah, separation is required. The discussion continues on the next amud.

defects.currentClaim: Adds a reason not in the source: 'since the atonement rites of Yom Kippur resemble those performed during the days of the inauguration'.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 32-34: 'bishlama... ela eima kulei kra b'Yom HaKippurim ktiv' with no stated reason.
defects.proposedReplacement: Granted, the whole verse cannot be set on the parah, since 'to atone' is written and the parah is not a matter of atonement. But say the whole verse is written about Yom Kippur? Then the parah kohen's separation would have no source here.

defects.sourceSupports: The verse and its split ('la'asot... l'chaper') are on lines 29-31; line 27 is only 'menah hanei milei'.
The verse and split are on lines 29-31.

defects.currentClaim: '...but the Gemara's own text then raises one further objection ('ve'eima', line 39) and breaks off before resolving it, so the derivation is not settled on this daf.'
defects.sourceSupports: Line 39 is outside s06 (27-38) by the boundary decision; s06 may say only that the discussion continues on the next amud.
defects.proposedReplacement: Leviticus 8:34 is the anchor: 'to do' (parah) and 'to atone' (Yom Kippur). The gezerah shavah ('tzivah'/'tzivah' with Num 19:2) identifies 'to do' with the parah and carries the inauguration's separation over to it. The discussion continues on the next amud.

defects.currentClaim: '...but the daf raises one more objection to this derivation ('ve'eima') and stops before answering it.'
defects.sourceSupports: Rests on line 39, outside lines 27-38.
defects.proposedReplacement: 'Tzivah' in the parah statute (Num 19:2); 'tzivah' in the inauguration verse (Lev 8:34). The shared word licenses reading 'to do' as the parah and carrying the inauguration's separation over to it.

defects.currentClaim: Misconception 'The gezerah shavah is the entire derivation' is effectively affirmed by its own correction ('the split reading ... proves nothing on its own; the gezerah shavah is what actually...'); incoherent, and wrong: the challenge concedes that 'to atone' is Yom Kippur.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 32-34 'bishlama' concede the verse cannot be all parah, i.e. 'to atone' (Yom Kippur) stands; lines 34-38 the gezerah shavah answers only the parah question.

proposedReplacement.misconception: The gezerah shavah replaces Rabbi Yochanan's reading, so 'to atone' no longer teaches the Yom Kippur separation.
proposedReplacement.correction: The Gemara's challenge concedes that 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. The gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' answers only the question about the parah, establishing that 'to do' refers to the parah and that its kohen is separated as at the inauguration.

defects.currentClaim: '...the split reading (line 30-31) ... by itself it proves nothing...'
defects.sourceSupports: The split is Rabbi Yochanan's derivation; the challenge accepts its Yom Kippur half and questions only the parah half.
defects.proposedReplacement: Students often read the challenge (lines 32-34) as rejecting Rabbi Yochanan's whole reading. It concedes that the verse cannot be entirely about the parah and asks only why it should not be entirely about Yom Kippur; the gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' answers that by tying 'to do' to the parah.

defects.currentClaim: Holds a description of a derivation plus a note about an objection at the end of the daf (line 39, outside the sugya range).
defects.sourceSupports: Contract: finalRuling is the halachic bottom line and is empty when the sugya is purely analytical. Lines 27-38 are a scriptural derivation, not a ruling.
